# World Nuclear Association: Cooling Power Plants

Updated: 4 Aug 2026.

## Key Findings
- All electricity generating options use water at some stage. Wind/solar have smallest water footprints; biomass/hydro largest.
- **Fossil fuels and nuclear consume significant water for cooling** in operational phase.
- Cooling required by steam-cycle plants determined by **thermal efficiency** — not fuel type.
- Nuclear additional requirement: **heat must continue to be removed after reactor shuts down**.
- Nuclear plants have **greater location flexibility** than coal (fuel logistics), allowing siting by cooling considerations.
- **Most common nuclear cooling: flow of seawater** (once-through).
- Two uses of water: (1) convey heat from core to steam turbines, (2) remove/dump surplus heat.
- ~**two-thirds of energy lost** in steam/Rankine cycle (intrinsic thermodynamic limit).
- Bigger temperature difference = more efficient. Desirable to site near very cold water.
- Large LWR loads **20-30 tonnes of fabricated uranium fuel/year** (vs several million tonnes of coal for comparable coal plant).
- If water limited and no coastal site: plants can be sited away from load, incurring transmission costs.
- Many plants (fossil and nuclear) have **higher net output in winter than summer** due to cooling water temperature differences.
